summary: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated readings. Systematic errors spoil accuracy and are not removed by repeating.
Leading zeros never count as significant; trailing zeros after a decimal point do. Sums keep the fewest decimal places, products the fewest significant figures.
Percentage errors always add, each multiplied by its power: %(A^pB^q/C^r) = p%A + q%B + r%C.
Every term in a correct equation has the same dimensions; dimensions convert units and derive power-law relations, but cannot give numerical constants or tell work from torque.
R^2 = A^2 + B^2 + 2ABcosθ; |A - B| ≤ R ≤ A + B; two equal vectors at 120° have a resultant equal to either.
vec A·vec B = ABcosθ (zero when perpendicular), |vec A×vec B| = ABsinθ (zero when parallel, equals the parallelogram area).
v = u + at, s = ut + (1)/(2)at^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as, sn = u + (a)/(2)(2n-1); slope of v–t = acceleration, area = displacement.
Projectile: T = 2usinθ/g, H = u^2sin^2θ/2g, R = u^2sin2θ/g; maximum range at 45°; complementary angles give equal ranges.

sections.title: Newton's laws of motion and the conditions of equilibrium
Impulse, linear momentum and its conservation
Work, energy and power; the work–energy theorem; conservation of energy

summary: Inertia is resistance to change of motion, measured by mass; vec F = dvec p/dt; action and reaction are equal, opposite and act on different bodies, so they never cancel.
A weighing machine reads m(g ± a) according to the direction of the acceleration; zero in free fall, mg at constant velocity.
Equilibrium of a rigid body needs zero net force and zero net torque; three concurrent forces in equilibrium obey Lami's theorem.
Impulse = change in momentum = area under the force–time graph; spreading the same impulse over more time lowers the force.
With no external force, total momentum is conserved: recoil, explosions, rockets and every collision.
W = Fscosθ; the net work equals the change in kinetic energy; K = p^2/2m; P = Fv.
Elastic collisions conserve KE (e = 1); perfectly inelastic ones stick together (e = 0) and lose the most KE; equal masses in an elastic head-on collision exchange velocities.
Limiting friction μsN is independent of area of contact; μk < μs; angle of repose = angle of friction, μs = tanθr.
terms: Principle of conservation of linear momentum

sections.title: Moment of inertia of a uniform rod and radius of gyration
Torque, rotational work, kinetic energy and power

summary: Moment of inertia I = Σ mr^2 depends on the mass, its distribution and the axis — not on the angular velocity; it is the rotational analogue of mass.
Uniform rod: ML^2/12 about the centre, ML^2/3 about an end; the centre gives the least I of all parallel axes (I = Icm + Md^2).
Radius of gyration k = √I/M: L/(2√3) about the centre and L/√3 about an end; k doubles when I quadruples.
Torque τ = rFsinθ (unit N m, never joule) and τ = Iα; a force through the axis gives no torque; a couple turns without translating.
Rotational work τθ, power τω, kinetic energy (1)/(2)Iω^2; rotational equations of motion mirror the linear ones.
Angular momentum L = Iω = mvrsinθ (J s); τ = dL/dt.
With zero external torque Iω is constant: the skater, the diver, planets moving faster near the Sun; K = L^2/2I rises when I falls.

sections.title: Pressure in a fluid; surface tension, surface energy and capillary action
Viscosity: Newton's law of viscous flow, Stokes' law and terminal velocity, Poiseuille's formula
Equation of continuity and Bernoulli's principle with applications

summary: Pressure in a liquid is P0 + hρ g, the same at one level, independent of the vessel's shape; Pascal's law multiplies force in a hydraulic lift; upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced.
Surface tension (N m⁻¹) equals surface energy per unit area (J m⁻²); it falls with temperature and with soap or detergent; a soap film has two surfaces.
Excess pressure is 2T/r in a drop and 4T/r in a soap bubble — the smaller the bubble, the higher the pressure.
Capillary rise h = 2Tcosθ/(rρ g): liquids that wet glass (acute angle, concave meniscus) rise; mercury (obtuse, convex) is depressed; a short tube never overflows.
Viscous force F = η A dv/dx; viscosity of liquids falls and of gases rises on heating; SI unit Pa s.
Stokes' drag 6πη rv leads to the terminal velocity 2r^2(ρ - σ)g/9η, proportional to r^2.
Poiseuille's flow Q = π Pr^4/8η l depends on the fourth power of the radius.
Continuity A1v1 = A2v2 and Bernoulli P + (1)/(2)ρ v^2 + ρ gh = constant: faster flow means lower pressure — venturimeter, Torricelli's √2gh, wing lift, atomisers.

sections.title: Angular quantities; centripetal acceleration and force
Motion in a horizontal and in a vertical circle
Simple harmonic motion: displacement, velocity, acceleration, restoring force, energy, period and frequency
Simple pendulum and spring–mass system; forced oscillation and resonance

summary: In uniform circular motion speed is constant but velocity is not; the acceleration v^2/r = ω^2r points to the centre, and the centripetal force does no work.
The centripetal force is supplied by a real force: friction on a level road (vmax = √μ rg), the normal reaction on a banked road (tanθ = v^2/rg), tension, gravity.
In a vertical circle on a string the least speeds are √gr at the top and √5gr at the bottom; the tension is greatest at the bottom, by 6mg more than at the top.
SHM: acceleration = -ω^2× displacement; x = Asin(ω t + φ), v = ω√A^2 - x^2; speed is greatest at the mean position, acceleration at the extremes.
Total energy (1)/(2)mω^2A^2 is constant; KE = PE at x = A/√2; each form of energy oscillates at twice the frequency.
Simple pendulum T = 2π√l/g (independent of mass, depends on g); spring T = 2π√m/k (depends on mass, independent of g).
Springs in series are softer, in parallel stiffer; half a spring is twice as stiff.
Forced oscillations take the driver's frequency; at resonance (driving frequency = natural frequency) the amplitude is greatest, more sharply so with less damping.
